question: Our ops team wants a live order-count screen that people glance at about once a minute, the source is already an event log, and we only have a batch scheduler with nobody on call overnight. What refresh setup would you pick and why?
key_points: About 10 second micro-batch
Staff act on roughly 1 minute latency
A 1 minute trigger would push the worst case past that minute
Team runs a batch scheduler with no overnight on-call

question: We get 50 million events a day. How much more compute does running a always-on streaming job cost compared with a daily batch run on the same 20 nodes?
key_points: Daily batch reads in 40 minutes on 20 nodes, about 13 node-hours
Streaming holds 20 nodes for 24 hours, 480 node-hours
Ratio about 36 to 1
Excludes state store, checkpoint storage and on-call cost

question: In a setup with a batch view and a live view, the batch side has complete hours 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00 for a product (120, 134, 141) and the live side has 11:00 (130), 12:00 (141) and 13:00 (57). What total does a query return and why not just add everything?
key_points: Total is 452
Take 395 from batch (120+134+141)
Live rows at or before the last batch hour are discarded
Add 57 from 13:00; batch preferred where it exists

question: How does handling reprocessing and correctness differ between running separate batch and speed code paths versus one job definition that runs both bounded and unbounded?
key_points: Two-path design gets correctness from the batch overwrite and reprocesses by rerunning batch
Single-path gets correctness from handling late data in the stream and reprocesses by replaying the log
Two-path needs a merge at the boundary hour; single path has one output table
Single path needs enough log retention to replay

question: In the windowed test with 60 second windows, an event with time 20 arrives at 140 and gets dropped. What would change if we allowed 120 seconds of lateness instead of 30?
key_points: That late event would be counted
First window ends up closing at 24 once the last event arrives
The next window stays open because the watermark only reaches 80

question: I compared my shadow run output with a recompute of the same day and found small differences of a few units on random keys. What does that usually mean, versus a mismatch on every key for one hour?
key_points: Few units on random keys means late events the shadow dropped but the bounded run kept
So the lateness allowance is too short
Diff on every key for one hour points to a skipped offset or partition
Zero rows for 24 hours is the release criterion

question: We have a 2 second latency requirement and our team likes the batch engine. If we set a 1 second trigger and each run takes about 1 second, will micro-batch do the job?
key_points: p50 near 1.5 s but p99 near 2.5 s
That exceeds the 2 s SLA on the tail
So record-at-a-time is needed
Tail latency is where the trigger model loses

question: Why can't I just shrink the micro-batch interval to 100 ms to get near real-time instead of adopting another engine?
key_points: Each cycle has fixed planning and offset commit cost of around 1 second
A 2 s trigger spends half its time on overhead; 100 ms almost all
Below about 1 second micro-batch stops paying
That is where record-at-a-time engines come in

question: After a crash my output table has two rows for the same window. What are the options to make the sink cope, and why would I prefer one over reading with a latest-row view?
key_points: Upsert sink keyed by product and window start overwrites earlier row
Transactional sink commits output with offsets
Read-side dedupe keeps latest emission per key using emitted_at
Dedupe view costs a window function on every query, so upsert is usual when supported

question: My job processes 2,000 events a second and checkpoints every 30 seconds. How many events might get replayed after a crash, and what happens if I drop the interval to 5 seconds?
key_points: Worst case replay is 60,000 events at 30 s
At 5 s replay shrinks to 10,000 events
Snapshot pause cost runs 6 times as often
Choose an interval around a tenth of the SLA, bounded by what the store can absorb
